Instructions can operate directly on memory

questions.text:
The code shows the same task written for two processors.

State which version is for the RISC processor and explain **two** reasons for your answer.

content.starter_code:
; Version X
ADD 4:1, 6:3

; Version Y
LOAD  A, 4:1
LOAD  B, 6:3
ADD   A, B
STORE 4:1, A

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Version Y is RISC (1)
- uses several simple instructions instead of one complex one (1)
- only LOAD/STORE access memory; ADD works on registers (1)
scheme.model_answer: Version Y. It breaks the task into several simple instructions, and only LOAD and STORE access memory while ADD uses registers; Version X does it all in one complex instruction that accesses memory directly.

questions.title: Pipelining
questions.text: Explain what is meant by **pipelining** and why it is easier with RISC than with CISC.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Several instructions are processed at the same time at different stages of fetch–decode–execute (1)
- RISC instructions are the same length / take one cycle, so stages take equal time (1)
- CISC instructions vary in length / cycles, so long instructions hold up the pipeline (1)
scheme.model_answer: Pipelining means fetching the next instruction while the current one is decoded and the previous one executed. RISC instructions are fixed length and take one cycle, so every stage takes the same time, whereas CISC instructions vary in length and cycles, so the pipeline stalls.

questions.title: Smartphone processor
questions.text: Explain why most smartphones use RISC processors.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Simpler circuits / fewer transistors (1)
- so less power / heat → longer battery life, no fan, smaller (1)
scheme.model_answer: RISC chips have simpler circuits with fewer transistors, so they use less power and produce less heat, giving longer battery life without a cooling fan.

questions.title: Two differences
questions.text: Give **two** differences between RISC and CISC.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two, both sides (1 each): few vs many instructions; simple vs complex; fixed vs variable length; one vs several cycles; load/store vs direct memory access; many vs fewer registers; easy vs hard pipelining; more vs fewer instructions per program; low vs high power. Do NOT accept CISC has more registers.
scheme.model_answer: 1 RISC has a small set of simple instructions, whereas CISC has a large set of complex instructions. 2 RISC instructions take one clock cycle, whereas CISC instructions take several.

questions.title: CISC and memory
questions.text: Explain why a program compiled for a CISC processor usually takes **less memory** than the same program compiled for a RISC processor.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- One CISC instruction carries out several operations (1)
- so the program has fewer instructions / shorter machine code (1)
scheme.model_answer: A single CISC instruction can load, process and store data, so the program needs fewer instructions and its machine code is shorter.

parts.title: Desktop
parts.text: Most gaming PCs use CISC (x86) processors. Give **two** reasons why.

scheme.model_answer: Most PC games are compiled for x86, so CISC keeps compatibility; the PC runs on mains power with fans, so higher power use and heat are not a problem.

scheme.mark_scheme: Programs need more instructions (1) → longer machine code / more RAM / more work for the compiler (1)
scheme.model_answer: Complex tasks need many simple instructions, so programs are longer and take more memory.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): small set of simple instructions; fixed length; one clock cycle each; load/store only access memory; many registers; easy pipelining; hard-wired, low power
scheme.model_answer: RISC has a small set of simple, fixed-length instructions that each take one clock cycle; only LOAD and STORE access memory, and it has many registers.

scheme.mark_scheme: Several instructions processed at once at different stages (1); one instruction completes every cycle once full / CPU not idle (1); RISC instructions same length and one cycle so stages balanced (1)
scheme.model_answer: While one instruction executes, the next is decoded and another fetched, so an instruction finishes every cycle. RISC instructions are fixed length and take one cycle, so each stage takes the same time.

parts.title: Registers
parts.text: Explain why RISC processors need many general-purpose registers.

scheme.model_answer: Arithmetic instructions can only use registers, so many registers are needed to hold data and avoid slow memory accesses.

summary: RISC and CISC processor architectures — what an instruction set is, the characteristics of RISC and CISC, how each executes the same task, pipelining, examples of processors that use each, and a full comparison with exam-style answers.

blocks.content: Every processor (CPU) can only carry out a fixed list of **machine-code instructions** — such as LOAD, ADD, STORE, JUMP and COMPARE. The design of this list, and of the circuits that carry it out, is called the processor's **architecture**.

The **complete set of machine-code instructions** that a particular processor can decode and execute. Each instruction has an **opcode** (what to do) and usually an **operand** (the data or address to use).

items.title: Why the architecture matters
items.content:
- It decides **how many instructions** a program needs and **how long** each one takes.
- It affects the **speed**, **power consumption**, **heat**, **cost** and **size** of the chip.
- Programs compiled for one instruction set **cannot run directly** on a processor with a different one (e.g. x86 software on an ARM phone).

items.title: Two design approaches
items.content:
- **RISC** — *Reduced* Instruction Set Computer: a **small** set of **simple** instructions.
- **CISC** — *Complex* Instruction Set Computer: a **large** set of **complex** instructions.

blocks.content: One "tick" of the processor's clock. The **clock speed** (e.g. 3 GHz = 3 000 000 000 cycles per second) is how many cycles happen each second. An instruction takes one or more clock cycles to execute.
A processor design with a **small set of simple instructions**, each of which is the **same length** and executes in **one clock cycle**. Complex tasks are built from **several simple instructions**.

items.title: Instructions
items.content:
- **Few, simple** instructions (often fewer than 100).
- **Fixed-length** instructions → easy and fast to **decode**.
- **Few addressing modes**.
- Most instructions execute in **one clock cycle**.

items.title: Registers and memory
items.content:
- **Load/store architecture**: only **LOAD** and **STORE** instructions access main memory; all calculations use **registers**.
- **Many general-purpose registers**, so data stays inside the CPU and memory is accessed less often.

items.title: Hardware and software
items.content:
- **Hard-wired** control unit — simple circuits, **fewer transistors**.
- Programs contain **more instructions**, so the **compiler** does more work and the machine code takes **more RAM**.
- Simple hardware → **low power consumption** and **less heat** → ideal for **battery-powered** devices.

blocks.title: Examples of RISC processors
blocks.content: **ARM** (almost all smartphones and tablets, Raspberry Pi, Apple M-series Macs), **RISC-V**, **MIPS**, **PowerPC**. Used in **mobile phones, tablets, embedded systems, smart TVs, IoT devices**.

A processor design with a **large set of complex instructions**. A **single instruction** can carry out **several low-level operations** (for example load from memory, calculate and store the result) and may take **several clock cycles**.

items.title: Instructions
items.content:
- **Many** instructions (hundreds or more), including specialised ones.
- **Variable-length** instructions → more complex decoding.
- **Many addressing modes**.
- Instructions take **different numbers of clock cycles**.

items.title: Registers and memory
items.content:
- Instructions can work **directly on data in memory** (memory-to-memory operations).
- **Fewer general-purpose registers** are needed.

items.title: Hardware and software
items.content:
- Complex control unit, often **microprogrammed** (microcode) — **more transistors**.
- Programs contain **fewer instructions** → **shorter machine code**, less RAM needed for code, simpler compiler.
- More complex hardware → **higher power consumption** and **more heat**.

blocks.title: Examples of CISC processors
blocks.content: **Intel x86 / x86-64** (Core i3/i5/i7/i9) and **AMD** (Ryzen) processors used in most **desktop PCs, laptops and servers**. Older examples: Motorola 68000, VAX.

theory.title: The same task on RISC and CISC

blocks.content: The task: **multiply** two numbers stored in memory locations 2:3 and 5:2 and **store** the result in 2:3.
MULT 2:3, 5:2        ; loads both values, multiplies them, stores the result
blocks.caption: CISC — one complex instruction (several clock cycles)

blocks.content:
LOAD  A, 2:3         ; copy first value into register A
LOAD  B, 5:2         ; copy second value into register B
PROD  A, B           ; multiply registers A and B, result in A
STORE 2:3, A         ; copy the result back to memory
blocks.caption: RISC — four simple instructions (one clock cycle each)

blocks.title: What the example shows
rows: Number of instructions in the program

blocks.content: **Time for a program = number of instructions × cycles per instruction × time per cycle.** CISC tries to make the **number of instructions** small; RISC tries to make the **cycles per instruction** small (ideally 1).

A technique in which the processor works on **several instructions at the same time**, each at a **different stage** of the fetch–decode–execute cycle — while one instruction is being executed, the next is being decoded and the one after that is being fetched.

Clock cycle:     1        2        3        4        5
Instruction 1:   Fetch    Decode   Execute
Instruction 2:            Fetch    Decode   Execute
Instruction 3:                     Fetch    Decode   Execute

Without pipelining: 3 instructions × 3 cycles = 9 cycles
With pipelining:    5 cycles — after the pipeline fills, one instruction finishes every cycle
blocks.caption: A three-stage pipeline (each column is one clock cycle)

items.title: Why RISC suits pipelining
items.content:
- Every instruction has the **same length** and takes **one cycle**, so each stage takes the **same time** and the pipeline flows smoothly.
- Simple decoding means each stage is quick.

items.title: Why CISC is harder to pipeline
items.content:
- Instructions have **different lengths** and take **different numbers of cycles**, so a long instruction **holds up** those behind it.
- Modern CISC chips (Intel, AMD) translate complex instructions into simple RISC-like **micro-operations** inside the CPU so they can be pipelined.

items.title: Advantages of RISC
items.content:
- Each instruction executes **quickly** (one cycle).
- **Pipelining** is efficient.
- **Low power and heat** → longer battery life, no fan needed.
- **Simpler, smaller, cheaper** chips.

items.title: Disadvantages of RISC
items.content:
- Programs need **more instructions** → larger code, more RAM.
- More work for the **compiler** / programmer of assembly code.

items.title: Advantages of CISC
items.content:
- **Fewer instructions** per program → shorter code, less memory.
- Easier to write **assembly code**; simpler compilers.
- **Backward compatible** — huge amount of existing x86 software.

items.title: Disadvantages of CISC
items.content:
- Complex instructions take **several cycles**; harder to pipeline.
- **More power and heat**; more expensive chips.
- Many complex instructions are **rarely used**.

blocks.title: Registers — a common trap
blocks.content: Remember: **RISC has many registers** (because all calculations happen in registers, and only LOAD/STORE use memory). CISC can work directly on memory, so it needs **fewer** registers. Do not say CISC has more registers.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Describe RISC architecture. [3]**
RISC uses a **small set of simple instructions** (1) of **fixed length** that each execute in **one clock cycle** (1); only **LOAD/STORE** access memory and it has **many registers** (1), so it is well suited to **pipelining** (1).

**Q: Give two differences between RISC and CISC. [2]**
RISC has a **small** set of simple instructions, **whereas** CISC has a **large** set of complex instructions (1). RISC instructions take **one clock cycle**, **whereas** CISC instructions may take **several** (1).

**Q: Explain why smartphones usually use RISC processors. [2]**
RISC processors have **simpler circuits / fewer transistors** (1), so they use **less power and produce less heat**, giving **longer battery life** without a fan (1).

**Q: Explain why CISC programs need less memory. [2]**
One CISC instruction can do **several operations** (1), so a program has **fewer instructions** and the machine code is **shorter** (1).

- Saying RISC is "slower because it has fewer instructions" — each instruction is **faster**; overall speed depends on the task.
- Saying CISC has **more registers** — RISC has more.
- Comparing only one side ("RISC has simple instructions") — a comparison needs **both** RISC **and** CISC.
- Mixing up **number of instructions in the set** (RISC fewer) with **number of instructions in a program** (RISC more).
